extracted.intended_audience: aspiring photographers, photo editors, and visual journalists seeking magazine/editorial work
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on what makes powerful visual journalism, how photo editors select and sequence images for magazines, and how photographers should present and produce work to get assigned. Includes career and production advice for working in editorial photography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial evaluation questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When people ask me, what do you do? I point to a picture in a magazine and say, look at this photo, how did this get here? Who chose the photographer and why? How did the photographer get access to the subject? Why did they choose to shoot in colour or in black and white? Who set up the shoot? What did the art director want? What did the editor want? What was the tone of this story? What did we want to convey to the reader? How were the photos chosen and placed in the layout?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the many decisions a photo editor must make when evaluating images and commissioning work; use them as an internal checklist to assess fit, access, aesthetic choices (color vs B&W), production logistics, editorial tone, and how images will read in sequence and layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-assigning fine art photographers for editorial work
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It used to be that you were either a photojournalist or a fine art photographer and it was her idea to get fine art photographers shooting editorial – it’s part of what’s called cross assigning.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may seek fine art photographers for editorial assignments to bring new perspectives and aesthetics; photographers should be open to editorial briefs and editors should consider non-traditional visual voices for stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational and production planning skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Being organised and good at planning so he would do these epic cross country trips where he’d go photograph in multiple locations and, just as a pal, I’d help him put together a list of places to go, places to stay, an itinerary, a budget proposal…
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong planning skills (itineraries, budgets, logistics) are valuable for photographers and photo editors; the ability to coordinate multi-location shoots and produce clear proposals increases the chance of assignment and successful execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy making things happen; be scrappy on small budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: At VICE, we would have a $1,000 budget to do a 10 page fashion shoot and I enjoyed that – making things happen, being scrappy, it was fun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to produce quality work under tight budgets and constraints is prized; demonstrate resourcefulness and a willingness to problem-solve in low-budget production scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular photographic style that stops the viewer
rubrics_metrics.description: You can tell when a photographer has a singular style. They make images that stop you in your tracks, images that you want to study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a distinctive, recognizable visual voice. Editors look for photographers whose work is compelling at first glance and rewards sustained viewing; style helps a photographer stand out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-service visual journalism / choosing projects that inform and create change
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘America at Hunger’s Edge… is an incredible example of public service journalism – creating change by informing people visually.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors value long-form, documentary projects that illuminate social issues and can have impact; projects that combine visual depth and reporting are strong editorial candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images must ‘read’ at magazine size (large-format readability)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Her photographs work at that size because you can read them, they’re so full. You start noticing things in the corner that add detail to these people’s complex lives.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select images that hold up when printed large (double-page spreads): rich, layered photos with details and compositional depth that reveal more on extended viewing are preferable for magazine features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work ethic: continual output and persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It’s not just about talent, though – the most successful photographers are workaholics. They are never not working. They almost have an obsessive need to do this.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained productivity and devotion to the craft are critical; editors favor photographers who continually make work, follow through on projects, and demonstrate long-term commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an easy-to-view, organized website with contact details
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘On a practical note, it’s really important to have an easy-to-view, organised website. It doesn’t have to be flashy – sometimes that’s a hindrance. Often we’re crashing stories and we need to find a photographer in a certain area immediately. I want to go to a website and quickly see portraits, documentary work, tearsheets so I can show a screengrab to my colleagues and – crucially – a phone number and email address so we can get in touch with you!’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep an uncluttered portfolio site that clearly displays relevant categories (portraits, documentary, tearsheets) and provides immediate contact info. Avoid overly flashy designs that hide work or slow access; enable editors to find and contact you quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be visible across discovery platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘We’re constantly looking at everything from Insta to journals, to websites, to art shows.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a presence across Instagram, journals, websites, and exhibitions so editors can discover your work in multiple contexts; diversify where your work appears to increase exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring openness to non-traditional photo editor backgrounds
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Kathy will often hire photo editors who don’t have photo editing backgrounds – people who come from law, for example, or the film industry.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial hiring can value transferable skills from other professions; candidates from varied backgrounds who bring organizational, critical, or storytelling abilities can succeed as photo editors.
